Abstract
Semantic segmentation is a crucial prerequisite in clinical
applications and computer-aided diagnosis. With the devel-
opment of deep neural networks, biomedical image segmen-
tation has achieved remarkable success. Encoder-decoder
architectures that integrate convolutions and transformers
are gaining attention for their potential to capture both
global and local features. However, current designs face
the contradiction that these two features cannot be contin-
uously transmitted. In addition, some models lack a uni-
fied and standardized evaluation benchmark, leading to sig-
nificant discrepancies in the experimental setup. In this
study, we review and summarize these architectures and an-
alyze their contradictions in design. We modify UNet and
propose WNet to combine transformers and convolutions,
addressing the transmission issue effectively. WNet cap-
tures long-range dependencies and local details simulta-
neously while ensuring their continuous transmission and
multi-scale fusion. We integrate WNet into the nnUNet
framework for unified benchmarking. Our model achieves
state-of-the-art performance in biomedical image segmen-
tation. Extensive experiments demonstrate their effective-
ness on four 2D datasets (DRIVE, ISIC-2017, Kvasir-SEG,
and CREMI) and four 3D datasets (Parse2022, AMOS22,
BTCV, and ImageCAS). The code is available at https :
//github.com/Yanfeng-Zhou/nnWNet.

2. Related Work
Convolution-Based Biomedical Image Segmentation.
The efficient and lightweight U-shaped CNNs are dominant
in biomedical image segmentation. They can retain the po-
sition information of the boundaries and alleviate overfitting
under the limited data volume of biomedical images. Some
studies add or improve various designs to the U-shaped
CNNs to better extract features. UNet++ [62] redesigns the
skip connection between the encoder and decoder to achieve
multi-scale feature aggregation. Attention UNet [37] inte-
grates the attention gate module into UNet [41] to better
focus on target structures of varying shapes and sizes. [45]
proposes a full convolutional U-shaped network (CMUNet)
that incorporates hybrid convolution and multi-scale atten-
tion gate. Furthermore, some studies have extended these
architectures to 3D to meet the needs of volumetric seg-
mentation. [36] proposes a fully convolutional 3D network,
VNet. ConResNet [55] proposes inter-slice context residual
learning to improve the ability of spatial context perception.
[57] proposes a low-frequency and high-frequency fusion
network, XNet, for fully- and semi-supervised biomedical
image segmentation.
Transformer-Based Biomedical Image Segmentation.
The transformer model treats images as sequences of small
patches. It employs a self-attention mechanism based on
fully connected networks to capture long-range dependen-
cies across the entire image and uses position encoding
to represent the spatial relationships between the patches.
Several studies have explored integrating transformers into
U-shaped architectures. Common strategies include: pure
transformer UNet without convolutional layers, such as
SwinUNet [5], D-Former [12], nnFormer [56]; replac-
ing the convolutional encoder or decoder with the trans-
former, such as TC-CoNet [8], ConvTransSeg [13], UN-
ETR [18], Swin UNETR [17], 3D UX-Net [32]; incorpo-
rating transformer-based bridges or bottlenecks between the
encoder and decoder, such as CoTr [50], MissFormer [24],
DCA [1], TransAttUNet [6]; stacking convolutional lay-
ers and transformer layers in series or parallel, such as
ConvFormer [14], H2Former [20], DuAT [46], MaxViT-
UNet [29]. Furthermore, some studies are focused on op-
timizing the self-attention mechanism to reduce compu-
tational costs and memory consumption, such as BRAU-
Net++ [30], UNETR++ [43]. However, these architectural
designs have the defect of alternating and confusing trans-
mission between global and local features. We discuss this
issue in more detail in Section 3.1.
nnUNet. nnUNet [25, 26] is an automatically config-
ured segmentation framework that sets image preprocess-
ing, data augmentation, and training hyperparameters. It
not only serves as an out-of-the-box segmentation solution
but also provides a unified benchmark for evaluating model
performance. In this study, we conduct a comprehensive
and fair comparison based on the nnUNet framework.

3.2. Integrating Transformers without Contradic-
tions
To integrate the transformer into the encoder-decoder archi-
tecture, and ensure that global and local features can be con-
tinuously transmitted without interruption and confusion,
we slightly adjust UNet [41] and propose WNet. Figure 2
shows an overview of WNet. WNet consists of two cas-
caded encoder-decoder architectures, performs Overlapped
Patch Embedding (OPE) on the input images, uses the Local
Scope Blocks (LSBs) to construct multi-scale encoding and
decoding layers, and introduces the Global Scope Bridges
(GSBs) between the encoding and decoding layers at each
scale. We employ convolutional layers as LSBs to extract
local details, and use transformer layers as GSBs to capture
long-range dependencies. LSBs and GSBs perform feature
fusion to exchange information at each encoding-decoding
scale. We explain the motivation of architecture design in
detail in the supplementary material.
Specifically, the overlapped feature embedding is im-
plemented by 3×3 convolutions with a stride of 1 and
down-sampling. LSBs are implemented by 3×3 resid-
ual blocks [21] with a stride of 1 and down/up-sampling.
GSBs are implemented by transformers with global atten-
tion mechanism. Feature fusion is implemented by channel
concatenation. We compare various attention mechanisms
and fusion strategies in ablation studies in Section 4.6. Note
that the local features based on LSBs contain implicitly po-
sitional relationships, and since LSBs and GSBs can ex-
change information, we do not introduce additional posi-
tional encoding in GSBs.

3.3. Calling for a Unified Evaluation Benchmark
Due to the diversity of biomedical images in terms of im-
age sizes, dimensions, modalities, imaging regions, pixel
(voxel) sizes, segmentation objects, data scales, and patho-
logical changes, there are significant differences even
among datasets for the same clinical application. It results
in a lack of standardized training and validation set divi-
sions and consistent evaluation metrics for evaluating per-
formance. Some studies attempt to refine image prepro-
cessing (such as image resampling and region of interest
cropping) and optimize key hyperparameters (such as patch
size and the number of training epochs) to ensure that their
models perform better.
In general, due to the lack of a unified evaluation bench-
mark, comparative experiments are no longer merely a com-
petition of model architectures. nnUNet [25, 26] is an au-
tomatically configured segmentation framework. More im-
portantly, it provides a unified benchmark for purely and
fairly comparing various architectures. We integrate WNet
into the nnUNet framework to standardize the experimental
setup.
4. Experiments
4.1. Datasets
We evaluate our model on four 2D datasets (DRIVE [44],
ISIC-2017 [9], Kvasir-SEG [27], and CREMI [12]) and four
3D datasets (Parse2022 [35], AMOS22 [28], BTCV [31],
ImageCAS [53]). Table 2 presents the details on their ex-
perimental setup. Additional information on these eight
datasets is presented in the supplementary materials. From
Table 2, these datasets cover different modalities, dimen-
sions, imaging regions, data scales, and segmentation ob-
jects. Evaluating model performance is more representative
and convincing.
4.2. Unified Evaluation Benchmark
We implement our model via nnUNet framework (version
2.3.1). Training and inference of all the models are per-
formed on one NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. All models are
trained from scratch. To balance training time and effect,
we use 2d and 3d_lowres trainer for 2D and 3D datasets,
respectively. The number of training epochs is set to 200
for 2D datasets and 500 for 3D datasets. We use five-fold
cross-validation to evaluate the segmentation results and use
the Jaccard index (Jaccard), Dice coefficient (Dice), 95th-
percentile Hausdorff distance (95HD), and average surface
distance (ASD) as performance metrics. Jaccard and Dice
emphasize pixel-wise accuracy, whereas 95HD and ASD
emphasize boundary accuracy. Furthermore, we only use
the output of models to evaluate performance without any
additional post-processing. Other configurations (such as
learning rate, loss function, patch size, and optimizer) are
the default in the nnUNet framework.

3.3. Calling for a Unified Evaluation Benchmark
Due to the diversity of biomedical images in terms of im-
age sizes, dimensions, modalities, imaging regions, pixel
(voxel) sizes, segmentation objects, data scales, and patho-
logical changes, there are significant differences even
among datasets for the same clinical application. It results
in a lack of standardized training and validation set divi-
sions and consistent evaluation metrics for evaluating per-
formance. Some studies attempt to refine image prepro-
cessing (such as image resampling and region of interest
cropping) and optimize key hyperparameters (such as patch
size and the number of training epochs) to ensure that their
models perform better.
In general, due to the lack of a unified evaluation bench-
mark, comparative experiments are no longer merely a com-
petition of model architectures. nnUNet [25, 26] is an au-
tomatically configured segmentation framework. More im-
portantly, it provides a unified benchmark for purely and
fairly comparing various architectures. We integrate WNet
into the nnUNet framework to standardize the experimental
setup.

4.6. Ablation Studies
To verify the effectiveness of each component, we perform
the following ablation studies on four 2D datasets.
Comparison of Different Self-Attention. Table 5 com-
pares the performance of adding different self-attentions to
GSBs, including depth-wise convolution (DW Conv) with
large kernel [32], pooling [52], and efficient multi-head self-
attention (E-MHSA) [15]. Pooling achieves better results.
We use pooling as self-attention to all relevant experiments
in Table 3.
Comparison of Fusion Strategies. Table 6 compares
different fusion strategies of global and local features. We
find that the channel concatenation used by the raw UNet
achieves better performance. We apply it to all relevant ex-
periments in Table 3.
Effectiveness of Combining Convolution and Trans-
former. We replace LSBs with PoolFormers and GSBs with
residual blocks to generate a pure transformer WNet and a
pure convolutional WNet, respectively. Table 7 compares
the performance of hybrid, pure convolutional, and pure
transformer architectures. Overall, the hybrid architecture
demonstrates superior results. Note that the pure convolu-
tional architecture may achieve better contour accuracy be-
cause convolution focuses on local details and is sensitive
to boundaries.
Necessity of Continuous Transmission of Global and
Local Features. We replace the encoder and decoder in the
raw UNet [41] to demonstrate the significance of continu-
ous transmitting global and local features. Specifically, we
implement pure convolution, pure transformer, series con-
nection of convolution and transformer, and parallel con-
nection of convolution and transformer to construct the en-
coder and decoder. Table 8 compares the performance of
these architectures. Our findings indicate that the series
connection has a negative effect. This may be due to the se-
ries connection forcing global and local features to be gen-
erated alternately, which hinders continuous transmission.
In contrast, the parallel connection and fusion before each
down-sampling yields positive results because it avoids the
conflict of capturing long-range dependencies from local
features while simultaneously extracting local details from
global features. The performance of using a convolutional
encoder with a transformer decoder is similar to that of
using a transformer encoder with a convolutional decoder,
with both architectures performing between the series and
parallel connections. Furthermore, we find that the combi-
nation of transformer and convolution outperforms the pure
convolutional architecture, further proving the necessity of
focusing on both global and local features.

spans.content: 5. Conclusion
We systematically summarize the transformer-based
encoder-decoder architectures for biomedical image seg-
mentation and analyze the contradictions within their
designs. To incorporate the transformer and address the
contradictions, we slightly adjust UNet and propose WNet.
WNet can capture long-range dependencies and local
details simultaneously and ensure their continuous trans-
mission and multi-scale fusion. We integrate WNet into the
nnUNet framework for unified benchmarking. Our model
achieves state-of-the-art biomedical image segmentation,
and extensive experiments on four 2D datasets and four 3D
datasets demonstrate its effectiveness.

spans.content: 5. Conclusion
We systematically summarize the transformer-based
encoder-decoder architectures for biomedical image seg-
mentation and analyze the contradictions within their
designs. To incorporate the transformer and address the
contradictions, we slightly adjust UNet and propose WNet.
WNet can capture long-range dependencies and local
details simultaneously and ensure their continuous trans-
mission and multi-scale fusion. We integrate WNet into the
nnUNet framework for unified benchmarking. Our model
achieves state-of-the-art biomedical image segmentation,
and extensive experiments on four 2D datasets and four 3D
datasets demonstrate its effectiveness.
